## <span class="dot dot-warning"></span> Watch Out — Starting Fresh? Run This First
If you're jumping into this module on a new day, or `raw_data` and
`raw_metadata` aren't in your environment, run this once before continuing:

```r
#| eval: false
metadata_url  <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv"
rawcounts_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv"

download.file(metadata_url,  destfile = "raw_data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
download.file(rawcounts_url, destfile = "raw_data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")

raw_metadata <- read.csv("raw_data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
raw_data     <- read.csv("raw_data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Convert README.txt to README.qmd

Your `README.txt` from Arc 2 is a snapshot — accurate the moment you wrote
it, and silently out of date the moment your folder structure changes.
Converting it to a `.qmd` file is our first step toward fixing that.

1. Find `README.txt` in your project folder and rename it to `README.qmd`
   (right-click → Rename on Windows, or select the file and press Return
   on Mac)
2. If you don't already have a `_quarto.yml` file in your project root,
   create one and add:

   ```yaml
   project:
     type: default
   ```

3. In your `README.qmd`, wrap your existing file-structure listing in
   triple backticks (```` ``` ````) so it's formatted as a code block

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — What Is Markdown?
The triple-backtick formatting you just used, along with things like
`#` for headings and `**bold**` for bold text, is called **Markdown** —
a simple, plain-text way to add formatting that any text editor can
read, with no special software required. A `.qmd` file is markdown text
with executable code chunks mixed in; strip the code out, and what's
left is a plain markdown document.
:::

4. In the terminal, run `quarto render`, then `quarto preview readme.qmd`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — What Is `localhost`?
The browser window that opens shows an address starting with `localhost`
followed by a port number. That means your own computer is serving the
file to itself — it is not on the internet, and no one else can see it.
This is how you preview a Quarto document before it's ever published
anywhere.
:::

## Automate the Project Tree

Right now your file tree is still just text you typed — exactly as
easy to go stale as it was in `README.txt`. This code chunk generates
and annotates it automatically, every time you render, so it can't.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-warning"></span> Watch Out — This One's Local-Only
`dir_tree()` reads your actual project folder from disk. There's no real
project structure to list inside a browser sandbox, so this chunk is
shown as a display only — paste it into your own `README.qmd` to see it
work.
:::

```r
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| results: asis

library(fs)

tree_output <- capture.output(dir_tree(".", recurse = 2))

comments <- list(
  "raw_data"       = " (original data goes here)",
  "processed_data" = " (clean data goes here)",
  "scripts"        = " (code goes here)",
  "outputs"        = " (results and charts go here)",
  "README.qmd"     = " (project documentation)"
)

for (item in seq_along(tree_output)) {
  line <- tree_output[item]
  for (name in names(comments)) {
    if (grepl(name, line)) {
      tree_output[item] <- paste0(line, comments[[name]])
      break
    }
  }
}

cat("```\n")
cat(paste(tree_output, collapse = "\n"))
cat("\n```\n")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — What This Script Does
- `dir_tree()` generates a visual tree of your project folder, two levels deep
- `capture.output()` stores that tree as a character vector your own code
  can modify — rather than text you'd have to retype by hand
- The `comments` list defines annotations for specific folders or files
- The `for` loop (from Arc 3) checks each line against every name in that
  list and appends a matching annotation where it finds one
- `cat()` prints the result back out as a formatted code block in your
  rendered document
:::

Paste this chunk into your `README.qmd` in place of your plain file tree,
wrapped in ```` ```{r} ```` instead of plain triple backticks. Re-render,
and your README now regenerates its own project structure every time —
try adding your own entry to the `comments` list and rendering again to
see it reflected.

## Your First Data Visualization in a `.qmd`

A `.qmd` file mixes narrative text with executable code chunks — when you
render it, the text and the live output of your code are woven together
into one finished document. You just saw this with your project tree;
here it is with a figure.

```{webr-r}
sample_cols <- grep("^GSM", colnames(raw_data), value = TRUE)

hist(raw_data[[sample_cols[1]]],
     main = paste("Distribution of counts:", sample_cols[1]),
     xlab = "Raw count")
```

Render the document to see the sentence above and the histogram below
combine into one finished file — change either one, and both update
together when you render again.

## Your Turn: Visualize a Range, Safely

Modify the function below so it only plots when there's actually data in
the requested range — using an `if`/`else` from Arc 3 to check first.

```{webr-r}
visualize_range <- function(df, sample_col, min_val, max_val) {
  values <- df[[sample_col]]
  in_range <- values[values >= min_val & values <= max_val]

  # TODO: add a check here — if length(in_range) is 0, print a message
  # like "No values found in that range" instead of calling hist()
  hist(in_range, main = paste(sample_col, ":", min_val, "to", max_val),
       xlab = "Raw count")
}

visualize_range(raw_data, sample_cols[1], min_val = 10, max_val = 1000)
```

<details>
<summary>Check your work</summary>

```r
visualize_range <- function(df, sample_col, min_val, max_val) {
  values <- df[[sample_col]]
  in_range <- values[values >= min_val & values <= max_val]

  if (length(in_range) == 0) {
    cat("No values found in that range\n")
  } else {
    hist(in_range, main = paste(sample_col, ":", min_val, "to", max_val),
         xlab = "Raw count")
  }
}
```
</details>

## From Figure to Methods Text

Everything so far has been browser-based, which means the narrative text
on this page can't actually react to the live code cells above it — only
a document you render yourself, on your own machine, can do that.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-warning"></span> Watch Out — This Won't Run on This Page
Inline code like <code>&#96;r min_val&#96;</code> only updates when *you* render a
`.qmd` file locally. The live cells on this website are compiled once,
ahead of time — changing a value in a browser cell above will never
change a sentence of text on this page. Try the block below in your own
`analysis.qmd` file instead, where it will.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tour"></span> Code Tour — Tying Your Figure to Your Text
In your own `.qmd` file, a code chunk can set values that your narrative
text then refers to directly:

```r
#| echo: false

sample_col <- "GSM3119015"
min_val <- 10
max_val <- 1000

values <- raw_data[[sample_col]]
in_range_idx <- which(values >= min_val & values <= max_val)
```

<pre><code>## Methods

Raw counts for sample &#96;r sample_col&#96; were examined in the range
&#96;r min_val&#96;–&#96;r max_val&#96;. This range contained &#96;r length(in_range_idx)&#96;
genes (row indices: &#96;r paste(head(in_range_idx, 5), collapse = ", ")&#96;,
among others).
</code></pre>

Change `min_val` and `max_val` in the code chunk, re-render, and watch
**both** the sentence and the figure update together — from the same two
numbers, in one place.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Why Row Indices, Not Gene Names, for Now
We haven't cleaned this dataset yet — that happens in Arc 5, which is
where readable gene symbols get attached to each row. For now, a row
index is a placeholder for "which gene," standing in for the moment you'll
replace it with `gene_symbol[in_range_idx]` once that column exists. This
is exactly the kind of methods-section sentence that, in a real paper,
needs to update itself the instant an upstream analysis choice changes —
which is the entire point of writing it this way instead of typing a
number by hand.
:::

## Extending Further: Publishing with a Journal Template

This next piece goes beyond what we'll build from scratch together
today — it's here so you know it's possible, and can come back to it on
your own.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tour"></span> Code Tour — Publishing with a Journal Template
This uses `tidyverse` and `scales`, which we haven't covered in depth
yet — that's coming in Arc 5. For now, treat `library(...)` simply as
"turn this set of extra functions on for this session."

**Formatting as a journal submission** — try this later, on your own
machine. Quarto extensions can format a document to match a specific
journal's submission requirements — layout, fonts, figure formatting —
without touching your analysis code at all. This part can't run in a
browser sandbox, since it installs files onto a real file system:

```bash
quarto add quarto-journals/plos
quarto use template quarto-journals/plos
```

This installs an extension that reformats your rendered output to PLOS
journal standards. The same approach works for other journals under
`quarto-journals` — the installation step changes, but your analysis
code underneath never has to.

**The analysis itself** — this part runs right here:

```{webr-r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(janitor)

gene_data <- rio::import(here::here("raw_data", "GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")) %>%
  clean_names()

gene_data_long <- gene_data %>%
  rename(ensembl_id = `...1`) %>%
  filter(!is.na(gene_symbol), gene_symbol != "") %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(ensembl_id, gene_symbol),
               names_to = "sample",
               values_to = "expression")

gene_variability <- gene_data_long %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol, ensembl_id) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_expression          = mean(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    variance                 = var(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    coefficient_of_variation = sd(expression, na.rm = TRUE) / mean_expression,
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

top_genes <- gene_variability %>%
  arrange(desc(variance)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

cat("Total genes analyzed:", nrow(gene_variability), "\n")
cat("Most variable gene:", top_genes$gene_symbol[1],
    "with variance =", round(top_genes$variance[1], 2), "\n")
```

```{webr-r}
heatmap_data <- gene_data_long %>%
  filter(gene_symbol %in% top_genes$gene_symbol) %>%
  left_join(top_genes %>% select(gene_symbol, variance),
            by = "gene_symbol") %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
  mutate(scaled_expr = scale(expression)[, 1]) %>%
  ungroup()

expression_heatmap <- heatmap_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sample,
             y = reorder(gene_symbol, variance),
             fill = scaled_expr)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red",
    name = "Scaled\nExpression", limits = c(-3, 3),
    oob = scales::squish
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Expression Variability Heatmap: Top 15 Most Variable Genes",
    subtitle = "Genes ordered by variance (highest at top)",
    x = "Sample ID", y = "Gene Symbol"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10, face = "italic"),
    legend.position = "right",
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

print(expression_heatmap)
# On your own machine, this line writes a real, timestamped .png to your
# outputs/ folder — the same automated file-naming pattern from Arc 2:
# ggsave(paste0("outputs/", timestamp, "_expression_heatmap.png"),
#        plot = expression_heatmap, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```
:::

## What We Did, and Why

**What we built:** converted a plain README into a self-updating Quarto
document, created a figure inside a `.qmd` for the first time, wrote a
function that safely checks before plotting, and read through a worked
example of a methods-section sentence that updates itself from the same
values driving a figure — plus a guided tour of a full publication-style
analysis.

**Why it matters:** your project's own documentation now regenerates
itself instead of going stale, and the gap between "the number in my
figure" and "the number in my methods text" — a classic, quiet source of
irreproducible papers — disappears when both come from the same chunk of
code instead of being typed twice, by hand, separately.
